p.src: Now Sun Quan wished to demand the return of Jingzhou. Zhang Zhao offered a plan: “The man Liu Bei relies upon most is Zhuge Liang. His elder brother, Zhuge Jin, now serves Wu. Why not detain Jin’s entire family and send him into Sichuan to tell his brother to persuade Liu Bei to surrender Jingzhou? He can say, ‘If it is not returned, my entire family will surely suffer for it.’ Mindful of the bond between brothers, Liang will certainly consent.” Sun Quan said, “Zhuge Jin is an honest gentleman. How could I bear to imprison his family?” Zhang Zhao replied, “If you secretly let him know that it is merely a stratagem, he will naturally be at ease.” Sun Quan followed his advice, summoned Zhuge Jin’s family, and placed them under nominal confinement in his residence; meanwhile, he composed a letter and dispatched Zhuge Jin to western Sichuan. Within a few days Zhuge Jin reached Chengdu and first sent a man to notify Xuande. Xuande asked Kongming, “Why has your elder brother come here?” Kongming replied, “Only to demand Jingzhou.” Xuande said, “How should we answer him?” Kongming replied, “We need only do thus and thus.”

p.src: Once their plan was settled, Kongming went beyond the city walls to welcome Zhuge Jin. Instead of taking him to his private residence, he led him straight to the guesthouse; when their greetings were over, Zhuge Jin burst into loud weeping. Liang said, “Brother, if something troubles you, only tell me. Why do you grieve so?” Jin replied, “My whole family is doomed!” Liang said, “Can it be because Jingzhou has not been returned? If your family has been seized because of me, how can my heart know peace? Do not worry, brother. I have a plan of my own for returning Jingzhou.” Overjoyed, Zhuge Jin accompanied Kongming to an audience with Xuande and presented Sun Quan’s letter. After reading it, Xuande angrily said, “Sun Quan gave me his sister in marriage, yet while I was away from Jingzhou, he secretly carried her off. Such conduct is intolerable! I was just about to raise the armies of Sichuan, march down upon Jiangnan, and avenge this wrong. Yet he still thinks of demanding Jingzhou from me?” Kongming fell to the ground, weeping and bowing, and said, “The Marquis of Wu has seized my elder brother’s entire family. If Jingzhou is not returned, my brother’s whole household will be put to death. If my brother dies, how can I alone go on living? For my sake, my lord, I beg you to return Jingzhou to Eastern Wu and preserve the bond between us brothers!” Xuande repeatedly refused, but Kongming continued to weep and plead. At length Xuande said slowly, “Since matters stand thus, for my military adviser’s sake I shall return half of Jingzhou: let him have the three commanderies of Changsha, Lingling, and Guiyang.” Liang said, “Since you have graciously consented, you may now write to Yunzhang and order him to hand over the three commanderies.” Xuande said, “Ziyu, when you reach him, you must appeal to my brother with gentle words. His temper is like a raging fire; even I fear him. You must take the utmost care.”

p.src: Having obtained the letter, Zhuge Jin took leave of Xuande, bade farewell to Kongming, and journeyed straight to Jingzhou. Yunzhang invited him into the main hall, where host and guest exchanged courtesies. Zhuge Jin produced Xuande’s letter and said, “The Imperial Uncle has agreed first to return three commanderies to Eastern Wu. I beg you, General, to surrender them this very day, so that I may return and report to my lord.” Yunzhang’s face changed. “My brother and I swore brotherhood in the Peach Garden and vowed together to uphold the House of Han. Jingzhou is the territory of the Great Han. How could so much as an inch of it be rashly given to another? ‘A general in the field need not obey every command of his sovereign.’ Though my brother has sent a letter, I still refuse to return the land.” Zhuge Jin said, “The Marquis of Wu has now seized my whole family. If Jingzhou is not returned, they will surely be put to death. I beg you, General, to take pity on them!” Yunzhang replied, “This is a deceitful stratagem of the Marquis of Wu. How could it deceive me?” Zhuge Jin said, “Why do you show me so little consideration, General?” Yunzhang grasped his sword and said, “Say no more! This sword of mine has no consideration for anyone’s face!” Guan Ping remonstrated, “This would reflect poorly upon the military adviser. I beg you to restrain your anger, Father.” Yunzhang said, “Were it not for the military adviser’s sake, I would see that you never returned to Eastern Wu!”

p.src: His face full of shame, Zhuge Jin hastily took his leave and boarded his boat. He returned to western Sichuan to see Kongming, only to find that Kongming had already departed on an inspection tour. Zhuge Jin could only seek another audience with Xuande and tearfully tell him how Yunzhang had threatened to kill him. Xuande said, “My brother is hot-tempered and exceedingly difficult to reason with. Ziyu, return home for the present. Allow me first to take the commanderies of eastern Sichuan and Hanzhong; then I shall transfer Yunzhang to guard them, and only then can Jingzhou be handed over.” Having no alternative, Zhuge Jin returned to Eastern Wu, appeared before Sun Quan, and related the whole affair. Sun Quan was furious. “Ziyu, after all your repeated journeys, could this entire affair be a scheme of Zhuge Liang’s?” Zhuge Jin replied, “No. My brother also wept and pleaded with Xuande, who only then agreed to return the three commanderies first. But there was nothing he could do when Yunzhang stubbornly refused.” Sun Quan said, “Since Liu Bei has said that he will first return the three commanderies, we can appoint officials and send them to take up their posts in Changsha, Lingling, and Guiyang. Then we shall see what happens.” Zhuge Jin said, “My lord’s words are most sound.” Sun Quan then ordered Zhuge Jin to take back his family, while appointing officials to assume office in the three commanderies.

p.src: Before many days had passed, every official sent to the three commanderies was driven back. They reported to Sun Quan: “Guan Yunzhang refused to receive us and drove us back to Eastern Wu during the night, threatening to kill anyone who lingered.” Sun Quan flew into a rage and sent for Lu Su to rebuke him: “Zijing, in former days you stood surety for Liu Bei when he borrowed Jingzhou from me. Now Liu Bei has gained western Sichuan and refuses to return it. How can you sit by and merely watch?” Lu Su replied, “I have already devised a plan and was just about to report it to my lord.” Sun Quan asked what the plan was, and Lu Su said, “Let us now station troops at Lukou and send someone to invite Guan Yunzhang to a meeting. If Yunzhang comes, I shall reason with him courteously. If he refuses to comply, we shall have swordsmen and axemen lying in ambush to kill him. If he refuses to come, we shall immediately advance our troops, fight him to a decision, and seize Jingzhou.” Sun Quan said, “That accords perfectly with my wishes. Carry it out at once.” Kan Ze stepped forward and said, “You must not. Guan Yunzhang is a tiger-like general unequalled in this age, no ordinary man can match him. I fear that if the affair goes awry, we shall instead suffer at his hands.” Sun Quan angrily said, “If we proceed like this, on what day shall we ever recover Jingzhou?” He immediately ordered Lu Su to carry out the plan without delay. Lu Su took leave of Sun Quan and went to Lukou, where he summoned Lü Meng and Gan Ning for consultation; he prepared a banquet in a riverside pavilion outside the Lukou camp, composed an invitation, selected an eloquent and quick-witted man from among his attendants as envoy, and sent him across the river by boat. At the river mouth Guan Ping questioned him, then conducted the envoy into Jingzhou. The envoy bowed before Yunzhang, fully explained Lu Su’s invitation to the meeting, and presented the letter. After reading it, Yunzhang said to the envoy, “Since Zijing has invited me, I shall come to the banquet tomorrow. You may return ahead of me.”

p.src: The messenger took his leave. Guan Ping said, “Lu Su’s invitation can mean no good. Why did you accept it, Father?” Yun-chang laughed. “Do you think I do not understand? Zhuge Jin has reported to Sun Quan that I refused to return the three commanderies. Sun Quan therefore ordered Lu Su to station troops at Lukou and invite me to a meeting, where he means to demand Jingzhou. If I do not go, they will call me a coward. Tomorrow I shall take a small boat with only a dozen attendants and go to the meeting armed with a single sword. Let us see how Lu Su dares approach me.” Guan Ping remonstrated, “Father, how can one whose person is worth ten thousand pieces of gold venture into a den of tigers and wolves? I fear this would not honor the trust my uncle placed in you.” Yun-chang replied, “Amid a thousand spears and ten thousand blades, under volleys of arrows and stones, I have ridden alone as though through an empty land. Why should I fear the rats of Jiangdong?” Ma Liang also remonstrated, “Though Lu Su has the bearing of an honorable gentleman, matters are now so urgent that he cannot avoid harboring other designs. You must not go there lightly, General.” Yun-chang said, “In the age of the Warring States, Lin Xiangru of Zhao had not the strength to bind a chicken, yet at the meeting at Mianchi he treated the sovereign and ministers of Qin as nothing. How much less should I fear, who have learned the art of facing ten thousand men? I have given my word and cannot break faith.” Ma Liang said, “Even if you go, General, preparations must be made.” Yun-chang replied, “Have my son select ten swift boats and conceal five hundred skilled marines aboard them to wait upon the river. When you see my red flag raised, cross the river at once.” Guan Ping received the order and went to make ready.

p.src: The messenger returned and reported to Lu Su that Yun-chang had readily accepted and would certainly arrive the next day. Lu Su consulted Lü Meng. “What shall we do when he comes?” Lü Meng said, “If he brings troops, Gan Ning and I shall each lead a force into ambush beside the bank. A cannon shot will be the signal to attack. If no troops come, we shall hide fifty axemen behind the hall and kill him at the banquet.” Their plan was settled. The next day Lu Su posted men at the landing to watch from afar. After the hour of the dragon, they saw a single boat upon the river. It carried only a few boatmen and sailors, and a red flag fluttered in the wind, displaying a great character “Guan.” As the boat drew near, they saw Yun-chang seated aboard in a blue headcloth and green robe. Beside him Zhou Cang held his great blade. Eight or nine burly men from west of the passes each wore a saber at his waist. Alarmed and suspicious, Lu Su received them into the pavilion. After exchanging courtesies they sat and drank, raising cups to one another, while Lu Su dared not look up. Yun-chang talked and laughed with perfect composure.

p.src: When they were half drunk, Lu Su said, “I have something to put before you, my lord. Pray hear me. Formerly your elder brother, the Imperial Uncle, had me guarantee before my lord that Jingzhou was only borrowed for temporary residence, with a promise to return it after taking Xichuan. Now Xichuan has been won, yet Jingzhou is not returned. Is this not a breach of faith?” Yun-chang replied, “This is an affair of state and need not be discussed at a banquet.” Lu Su said, “My lord possessed only the small territory of Jiangdong, yet lent you Jingzhou because he pitied you and your companions, defeated and come from afar, with no resources to sustain you. Now that Yizhou is yours, Jingzhou should naturally be returned. Yet the Imperial Uncle offers only three commanderies, and you refuse even that. I fear such conduct cannot be justified.”

p.src: Yun-chang said, “At the battle of Wulin, the General of the Left personally braved arrows and stones and exerted all his strength to defeat the enemy. Was he to labor in vain without receiving a foot of land for support? And now you come again to demand the territory?” Lu Su replied, “That is not so. When you and the Imperial Uncle were first defeated together at Changban, your plans exhausted and strength spent, you meant to flee far away. My lord pitied the Imperial Uncle for having nowhere to dwell and did not begrudge him the land. He gave him a place of refuge so that he might accomplish future deeds. But the Imperial Uncle has betrayed virtue and ruined friendship: having gained Xichuan, he still occupies Jingzhou. His greed and breach of honor will, I fear, draw the laughter of the realm. The Imperial Uncle is as yourself; how can you disclaim responsibility?”

p.src: Before Yun-chang could answer, Zhou Cang cried sternly from below the steps, “The lands beneath Heaven belong to those of virtue. Should Eastern Wu alone possess them?” Yun-chang changed countenance and rose. Snatching the great blade from Zhou Cang, he stood in the courtyard, glared at him, and shouted, “This is an affair of state. How dare you speak out of turn! p.src: Now Cao Cao was about to set out on a southern campaign when his military adviser Fu Gan, styled Yancai, submitted a memorial urging him to desist. The memorial said in substance: “I have heard that military action must be preceded by awe, and civil rule by virtue. Only when awe and virtue sustain each other can the work of kingship be achieved. When the realm was formerly in great disorder, Your Excellency used arms to quell it and pacified nine-tenths of the land. Those who have yet to accept the royal command are only Wu and Shu. Wu is protected by the perilous Yangzi, and Shu by lofty mountains; they are difficult to subdue by force. In my humble view, you should cultivate civil virtue, lay aside armor and cease hostilities, rest the army, nourish the soldiers, and await the time to act. u.src: Now Cao Cao was about to set out on a southern campaign when his military adviser Fu Gan, styled Yancai, submitted a memorial urging him to desist.
The memorial said in substance: “I have heard that military action must be preceded by awe, and civil rule by virtue.
Only when awe and virtue sustain each other can the work of kingship be achieved.
When the realm was formerly in great disorder, Your Excellency used arms to quell it and pacified nine-tenths of the land.
Those who have yet to accept the royal command are only Wu and Shu.
Wu is protected by the perilous Yangzi, and Shu by lofty mountains; they are difficult to subdue by force.
In my humble view, you should cultivate civil virtue, lay aside armor and cease hostilities, rest the army, nourish the soldiers, and await the time to act.

If you now raise hundreds of thousands and encamp beside the Yangzi, and the enemy hides deep behind its natural defenses, our men and horses will have no chance to display their ability, nor our ingenious changes any scope to exert their power; thus Heaven’s majesty will be humbled.
I pray Your Excellency examine this carefully.”

p.src: After reading it, Cao Cao abandoned the southern campaign, established schools, and invited and honored men of letters. Then the four Palace Attendants Wang Can, Du Xi, Wei Kai, and He Qia proposed that Cao Cao be honored as King of Wei. Xun You, Director of the Secretariat, said, “That must not be done. The Chancellor has risen to Duke of Wei and received the honor of the Nine Bestowments; his rank has already reached its summit. To elevate him now to the rank of king would be contrary to reason.” When Cao Cao heard, he angrily said, “Does this man mean to imitate Xun Yu?” When Xun You learned of this, anxiety and indignation made him ill. He lay sick for more than ten days and died at the age of fifty-eight. Cao Cao buried him with great honors and dropped the matter of becoming King of Wei.

p.src: Hearing this, Cao Cao glared angrily at the Emperor and departed in bitter resentment. Some of the attendants reported to the Emperor, “We have lately heard that the Duke of Wei intends to make himself king; before long he will surely usurp the throne.” The Emperor and Empress Fu wept bitterly together. The Empress said, “My father, Fu Wan, has long wished to kill Cao Cao. I shall now write him a letter and secretly plan the deed with him.” The Emperor said, “Formerly, because Dong Cheng did not keep his undertaking secret, he brought a terrible disaster upon himself; if this scheme should also leak out, both you and I are finished!” The Empress replied, “Day and night we sit as though upon a bed of needles. A life like this is worse than an early death! Of all the eunuchs, none seems more loyal and trustworthy than Mu Shun. We should have him carry this letter.” They immediately summoned Mu Shun behind the screen and dismissed all the attendants nearby. The Emperor and Empress wept bitterly and told Mu Shun, “The traitor Cao Cao intends to become King of Wei and will surely usurp the throne sooner or later. We wish to have the Empress’s father, Fu Wan, secretly plot against this traitor, but all those around us are his trusted henchmen, and there is no one we can rely upon. We want you to deliver the Empress’s secret letter to Fu Wan. Knowing your loyalty and honor, we are certain you will not betray us.” Mu Shun wept and said, “Your servant is deeply moved by Your Majesty’s great favor. How could I fail to repay it with my life? I beg leave to depart at once.”

p.src: The Empress then wrote the letter and gave it to Mu Shun. Mu Shun concealed it in his hair, slipped secretly out of the imperial palace, went straight to Fu Wan’s residence, and presented the letter. Seeing that it was in Empress Fu’s own hand, Fu Wan said to Mu Shun, “The traitor Cao Cao has a great many henchmen; we cannot act against him rashly. We must first have Sun Quan in the Southlands and Liu Bei in the Riverlands raise armies outside. Cao Cao would then be compelled to go against them in person. At that time we could seek out loyal and honorable ministers at court and plot together with them. With attacks from within and without, we might hope to succeed.” Mu Shun said, “Your Imperial Highness should write a reply to the Emperor and Empress, requesting a secret edict. Men can then be sent covertly to Wu and Shu to arrange a concerted rising, destroy the traitor, and rescue the sovereign.” Fu Wan at once took paper, wrote a letter, and gave it to Mu Shun. Mu Shun hid it in his topknot, took leave of Fu Wan, and returned to the palace.

p.src: But someone had already informed Cao Cao. Cao Cao was waiting beforehand at the palace gate. On his return Mu Shun encountered Cao Cao, who asked, “Where have you been?” Mu Shun replied, “The Empress is ill and ordered me to fetch a physician.” Cao Cao said, “Where is the physician you summoned?” Mu Shun said, “I have not yet managed to bring one.” Cao Cao shouted to his attendants to search Mu Shun all over. Finding nothing concealed on him, they let him pass. Suddenly a gust of wind blew off Mu Shun’s cap. Cao Cao called him back, took the cap, and examined it. After inspecting it thoroughly and finding nothing, he returned it and told Mu Shun to put it on. Mu Shun took it in both hands and put it on backward. Cao Cao grew suspicious and ordered his attendants to search Mu Shun’s hair, where they found Fu Wan’s letter. When Cao Cao read it, he saw that it proposed enlisting Sun Quan and Liu Bei as outside allies. Cao Cao flew into a rage, had Mu Shun seized and questioned in a secret chamber, but Mu Shun refused to confess. That very night Cao Cao mustered three thousand armored troops and surrounded Fu Wan’s private residence, arresting young and old alike; they found the letter written in Empress Fu’s own hand, whereupon all three clans of the Fu family were cast into prison. At dawn Cao Cao sent Xi Lü of the Imperial Guard into the palace bearing the insignia of authority, first to confiscate the Empress’s seal and ribbon.

p.src: That day the Emperor was in the outer hall when he saw Xi Lü lead three hundred armored soldiers straight inside. The Emperor asked, “What is the matter?” Xi Lü said, “By order of the Duke of Wei, I have come to confiscate the Empress’s seal.” The Emperor knew the plot had been exposed, and his heart and courage shattered. Xi Lü entered the inner palace just as Empress Fu was rising. He summoned the keeper of the seal and ribbon, demanded the jade seal, and departed with it. Knowing the affair had come to light, Empress Fu hid inside a partition wall in the pepper chamber behind the hall. Soon afterward, Hua Xin, Prefect of the Masters of Writing, led five hundred soldiers into the rear hall and asked the palace women, “Where is Empress Fu?” All the palace women claimed not to know. Hua Xin ordered the soldiers to break open the vermilion doors, but their search found no trace of her; guessing that she was inside the wall, he shouted to the armored men to break it open and search. Hua Xin seized the Empress by her topknot with his own hands and dragged her out. The Empress said, “I beg you to spare my life!” Hua Xin rebuked her, “Go and plead your case before the Duke of Wei yourself!” With her hair disheveled and her feet bare, the Empress was shoved out by two armored soldiers.
